1:
What the prophet is handed is a brick, not a roof tile. Clarke insists on the distinction and cites an ancient authority on the standard dimensions, two feet by one and four inches thick, the only size that makes the drawing possible. Gill prefers a green unbaked brick as easier to cut, and canvasses the reasons offered — that cities are built of brick, that the material bespeaks how easily the place could be knocked down, that it was meant to recall brickmaking in Egypt — before settling on the likeliest, that the Babylonians wrote on tiles, one authority reporting centuries of astronomical observation preserved so. Ellicott confirms the practice from the buried libraries that have given us most of what we know of those cities.

Ellicott enters a caution that shapes everything after. Drawing on soft clay is possible, but reading the whole run of these chapters he thinks the acts were described rather than performed. Henry takes the object emblematically instead: a city once engraved on the divine palms, whose tribal names were cut in precious stones on a priest's breastplate, is now worth only a brittle piece of clay, and it is laid where the eye can work on the heart. Wesley reduces the command to drawing a map.

Calvin turns the scene into an argument about signs. The performance would be childish theatre except that it was commanded, from which he draws the rule that a sacrament is distinguished from an empty show by nothing but the word of God: divine authority is what gives such things weight, and whatever men add is frivolous. He applies the rule sharply to the ceremonies of Rome, which he calls trifles precisely because they were devised to dazzle simple people without any command behind them.

The siege works are described from two directions. Calvin sketches ancient practice — mounds thrown up to fill trenches, wooden towers moved forward so troops could mass close in, machines since made obsolete by firearms. Clarke stops on the ram, which he says is first mentioned here: a long beam headed with brass shaped like a ram, slung on ropes between uprights so that it could be hauled back and released against the wall by a gang of men. He notes its absence from the siege of Troy and its later appearance in a Carthaginian siege recorded by a Roman writer.

Ellicott asks how likely such a siege looked at the time. Egypt was beaten out of contention, Babylon alone could mount one, and Babylon had already conquered the country three times in a few years, carried off two kings in chains and ten thousand of the leading people, and installed a puppet from the royal house. Only a fresh revolt could bring the armies back, and a fresh revolt was plain infatuation — which is exactly what followed.

The iron plate divides them. Clarke and Ellicott agree on the object, a flat griddle for baking cakes rather than a pan, and on its use: set upright it pictures a wall better than any vessel could, and it stands for the strength of the besieging lines and the impossibility of breaking out by a sally, so that the enemy is as unassailable as he is irresistible. Wesley transfers the hardness to the besiegers' patience. Henry finds instead a double meaning, an obstinacy on both sides of the iron — invaders resolved never to withdraw and defenders resolved never to capitulate. Gill collects further readings without choosing: the metal for the hardness of the people's hearts and its colour for the blackness of their sins, or a frying pan for the miseries of the captivity and the burning of the city, or simply the settled anger of God. Ellicott adds that Israel here means the whole nation, Judah standing for what the earlier deportations had left.
4:
Whether the lying was done or only seen is the standing question. Clarke has no doubt it happened: the man lay chained to a couch on his left side for three hundred and ninety days, then on his right for forty. Calvin and Wesley both take it for vision, Calvin saying so in passing while describing the dress. Gill sets out both cases and calls neither contemptible, noting that nobody could lie so long without a miracle, and that a later notice shows the prophet sitting at home before the term could have run out, the interval between the two dated points falling short even before the preliminary week is deducted.

Clarke supplies a key. The prophet stands for the nation, his lying down for its prostration, his bonds for its helplessness in captivity; the days count as years, a day apiece, through which the punishment due to sin is borne. The longer term he makes do double duty, marking both the length of the siege and the length of the exile. Wesley reads the number as measuring two things at once, how long the offence had been endured and how long the penalty would run.

Ellicott is careful about the idiom and candid about a difficulty. To bear the iniquity of another is a standing expression for suffering punishment due to sin, so the prophet stands for the people under judgment — which sits oddly beside his standing also for the besiegers who inflict it. He does not smooth this over but says plainly that such inconsistencies are common in symbolic action and spoil nothing. He also notes that the two houses are expressly distinguished, and explains the left side as the north because the Oriental takes his bearings facing east.

Calvin looks past the mechanics to the purpose. The people thought themselves punished beyond their deserts, which he calls the habit of hypocrites: not daring to plead innocence outright, they grumble that the affliction is excessive and offer something by way of composition, expecting that on strict equity they would escape or suffer less. Those left at home had grown the more stubborn for being spared, as though their account with God were closed, while the deportees complained of severity.

The arithmetic is attempted from several directions and no two agree. Wesley starts the longer count at a king's lapse into idolatry in the twenty-seventh year of his reign and ends it in the fifth year of the last captivity. For the forty, Clarke reports a reckoning that sums the idolatrous portions of six reigns to make exactly forty years, and adds that forty days may equally be the time taken to sack the city and temple. Wesley counts the same forty from a covenant renewal to the temple's destruction, a period through which punishment was deferred. Gill records the further question whether the forty lie inside the longer count rather than after it, which several expositors have held.

The posture is then fixed. Gill and Ellicott read the set face as inflexibility, Ellicott noting it is a favourite phrase of this prophet and that no relenting is to be looked for. On the bared arm they agree the sleeve of a loose robe is pushed back, Ellicott adding that it is bared for battle and Calvin describing a coat pulled half off to free one arm; Wesley has it stretched out ready to strike. Calvin admits the whole performance would be frigid — a man baring his arm at a painted city — were the meaning not attached to the figure. The bands close it: Gill takes them for the besiegers held to their work by providence rather than the besieged, an emblem of an unalterable decree, and Ellicott says the same of the prophet, that not pity only but weariness was to be shut out.
9:
The grain mixture is read as a famine ration. Gill notes that only the first two were ever human bread, the rest cattle food except in extremity; Clarke recognises the practice of eking out finer grain with coarser; Henry is blunter, calling it what horses and hogs are fed, and comparing the sack to a beggar's bag filled a handful at a time from different doors. Ellicott adds that the grains run from best to worst, so every kind would be sought, and that mixing them in one vessel violated at least the spirit of the law. Calvin grades the same scale: wheat for ordinary bread, barley or vetches for a poor region, lentils and beans and millet for severer want. Wesley says all of it will be little enough.

The daily allowance is then weighed. Gill and Wesley reckon the twenty shekels at ten ounces, Gill from an ancient historian's half-ounce shekel; Clarke turns the stock into three hundred and ninety daily loaves and puts the water at a pint and a half. Ellicott, working from a heavier shekel of some two hundred and twenty grains, gets under eleven ounces and calls it scarcely enough to live on, notes that food weighed rather than measured is itself the mark of scarcity, and reads the phrase about time as one daily issue. He observes too that only the longer term is named though the rule must have covered both. Calvin marks the water as the worse threat: wanting wine is hard, wanting water the last stage of famine.

The fuel is what the commentators find hardest. Gill has the cakes baked under ashes rather than in an oven, the ashes neither wood nor straw nor turf. Clarke explains that dried dung is ordinary fuel in the East and offers a mitigation: it never touched the bread, only heating the plate the cakes lay on, which he thinks removes the horror and most of the disgust. What it shows is that people unable to go outside the walls for beast-dung would be driven to the other kind.

Ellicott shifts the offence from the physical to the ceremonial: cakes baked in hot ashes take defilement from the fuel, so the objection is not squeamishness but law. He also meets the strongest argument against his reading. The phrase about doing it in their sight has been taken to prove a real act and not a vision; Ellicott answers that the public performance can itself be part of what was seen. Wesley states the same conclusion flatly.

The plea and the concession are handled kindly. Calvin insists the objection was not palate but lawfulness, and that a man who had fed carelessly could not have prayed so. Clarke and Ellicott both hear the protest echoed in an apostle's later refusal, Ellicott drawing the contrast that the apostle was told the ceremonial rule had lapsed while for the prophet it stood. Ellicott states the design plainly: the law had fenced them so thoroughly that exile among the nations must defile them, the condition obstinate sin ends in, further transgression made unavoidable. Gill notes that the prayer was heard and the terms eased, Ellicott that the substitute is the country's ordinary fuel.

The plain statement comes last. Ellicott takes bread for food in general, particular for whole. Calvin distinguishes two punishments in the broken staff, since even a sufficient supply may be robbed of strength, and cites the law's gloss, ten women baking in one oven and the bread returned by weight so that men eat and are not filled. Clarke, following another writer, matches the years back to the reign in which national idolatry began and the days to the siege itself, less the months the besiegers spent away against Egypt. Wesley closes on the symmetry: those who would not serve God cheerfully in plenty were made to serve enemies in want.
